```{r}
#| label: data
#| include: false
q <- load_quarterly()
panel <- q |>
  filter(qtr <= yearquarter("2019 Q4")) |>
  transmute(quarter = gsub(" ", "", format(qtr)),
            observation_date = as.Date(qtr) + months(2),
            CPIAUCSL = cpi, UNRATE = unrate, TB3MS = tbill, inflation = infl) |>
  as.data.frame()
stopifnot(nrow(panel) == 240, !anyNA(panel), !anyDuplicated(panel$quarter))
initial <- subset(panel, quarter <= "1999Q4")
stopifnot(nrow(initial) == 160)
series <- c("inflation", "UNRATE", "TB3MS")
series_names <- c("CPI inflation", "Unemployment", "3-month T-bill rate")
```

```{r}
  mutate(across(c(origin, target), format)) |>
  write.csv("results/forecasts.csv", row.names = FALSE)

scores <- evaluate_forecasts(results, benchmark = "4Q average")
```

# Data and preliminary evidence

<!-- OWNER: TBD. Draft below is condensed from Stages 1 and 2; revise as
needed. Template limit: no more than three main-text figures. -->

## Variables and construction

We use three monthly FRED series from the instructor-provided course files:
headline CPI (`CPIAUCSL`, seasonally adjusted, 1982-84 = 100), the civilian
unemployment rate (`UNRATE`, percent), and the three-month Treasury bill rate
(`TB3MS`, percent, discount basis). Each quarter takes its quarter-end month
(March, June, September, or December), so each quarterly value is the level at
the end of that quarter rather than an average across months.

Inflation is annualized quarter-over-quarter CPI growth,

$$
\pi_t=400\log\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}\right),
$$

where $P_t$ is end-of-quarter CPI. The log ratio is the quarterly growth rate;
multiplying by 100 converts it to percent and by 4 annualizes it. If CPI rises
from 100 to 101, $\pi_t=400\log(1.01)\approx 3.98$ percent. December 1959 CPI
is the base for 1960Q1. The CPI level trends upward throughout, while inflation
is its growth rate and has no trend.

## Exploratory evidence

```{r}
#| label: fig-initial
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "Initial-sample time plots and ACFs, 1960Q1-1999Q4. Dashed ACF bands are approximate 95% white-noise bounds."
par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(3.1, 3.6, 2.1, 0.8), mgp = c(2, 0.65, 0),
    cex = 0.78)
for (j in seq_along(series)) {
  y <- initial[[series[j]]]
  plot(ts(y, start = c(1960, 1), frequency = 4), ylab = "Percent",
       xlab = "", main = series_names[j], col = "#246B8E", lwd = 1)
  acf(y, lag.max = 24, main = "", xlab = "Lag (quarters)")
  title(main = "ACF", line = 0.5, font.main = 1)
}
```

All three series are highly persistent in @fig-initial. The mean of inflation
also shifts over 1960-1999. The number of PELT/BIC breaks depends on the noise
assumption, but every specification places breaks at 1973Q1 and 1981Q4, the
start and end of the high-inflation period.

| Series | Plot and dependence evidence | ADF/KPSS and break evidence | Working classification | Modeling implication |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| CPI inflation | Very persistent; long swings in level | ADF rejects only after differencing; KPSS rejects in levels; mean breaks in 1973Q1 and 1981Q4 | $I(1)$, provisionally | Motivates changing-mean models |
| Unemployment | Long business-cycle swings | Same test pattern | $I(1)$, provisionally | Interpret Phillips-curve and VAR level models with care |
| Treasury bill rate | Tracks inflation; early-1980s peak | Same test pattern | $I(1)$, provisionally | VAR level specification is a limitation |

These are working classifications, not proof of a permanent unit root. A
shifting mean can make a series that is stationary within periods fail
stationarity tests over the full sample. A fixed historical inflation level is
therefore not credible, which matters for AR($p$) models with a single long-run
mean. Full test output is in Appendix C.

# Forecasting design

<!-- OWNER: Dawson. Draft condensed from Stage 2, Step 2. -->

## Periods and information flow

| Period | Role |
|---|---|
| 1960Q1-1999Q4 | Initial analysis, design, and estimation |
| 2000Q1-2019Q4 | Historical out-of-sample comparison and selection |
| 2020Q1-2026Q2 | Final evaluation and monitoring |

During the historical comparison, every model is re-estimated on an expanding
window. At a forecast origin $T$, a model sees only quarters 1960Q1 through
$T$; lag selection, local-mean construction, and estimation all use that
sample. The first origin is 1999Q4. The origin then moves forward one quarter
at a time. Variables, transformations, candidate lag ranges, estimation
methods, and horizons stay fixed; only fitted parameters and BIC-selected lag
orders update. After selection, the chosen model is estimated once through
2019Q4 and kept fixed for the post-2020 evaluation.

## Targets and horizons

The target is inflation in the single quarter $T+h$. We forecast only
$h=1,4,8$. The historical exercise uses the common first origin 1999Q4 and the
common final target 2019Q4, so the target periods are 2000Q1-2019Q4 (80
errors) at $h=1$, 2000Q4-2019Q4 (77) at $h=4$, and 2001Q4-2019Q4 (73) at
$h=8$. One shared evaluation harness (Appendix A) produces every model's
forecasts on this schedule.

## Accuracy measures and planned tests

The error is actual minus forecast, $e_t=\pi_t-\hat\pi_t$, so a positive error
means underprediction. We report RMSE, relative RMSE against the
four-quarter-average benchmark, MAE, and mean error. RMSE is the primary
criterion because it penalizes large misses; MAE shows whether a few large
errors drive RMSE, and mean error shows systematic over- or underprediction.

## Diagnostics affecting interpretation

<!-- OWNER: Dawson. Condensed from Stage 2, Step 5; full output in
Appendix C. -->

The leading estimated Stage 2 one-step model, the gap AR, leaves no detectable
autocorrelation in its residuals (Ljung-Box $Q(8)=7.19$, $p=0.21$). Its error
variance is not constant: the residual standard deviation is about 1.2-1.4
percentage points in calm periods and 2.6-3.1 in 1973-1986 and 2005-2019. A
few energy-driven shocks dominate RMSE; dropping 2008Q4 alone lowers its
one-step RMSE from 3.06 to 2.28. Small RMSE differences between models should
therefore be read with care.

# Assessment of the paper-based ideas and monitoring

<!-- OWNERS: Sarat (Claims 1-4), Dawson (Claim 5). For each claim report

1. **A simple benchmark is difficult to beat consistently.**
2. **Allowing the typical inflation level to change improves forecasts.**
3. **More complex models are not automatically more accurate.**
4. **There is no universal winner.**
5. **The selected model remained stable after 2020.**

# Appendix C - Supporting diagnostics {.unnumbered}

## Stationarity tests {.unnumbered}

<!-- OWNER: TBD. Ported from Stage 2, Step 1. -->

For each ADF regression we use an intercept and no trend, selecting 0-4
augmentation lags by BIC on a common sample. KPSS tests use a constant and the
short bandwidth. The 5% critical values are -2.880 (ADF) and 0.463 (KPSS).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stationarity
test_series <- function(y) {
  differences <- embed(diff(y), 5)
  regression_data <- data.frame(change = differences[, 1],
                                level = y[5:(length(y) - 1)], differences[, 2:5])
  names(regression_data)[3:6] <- paste0("lag", 1:4)
  bic <- sapply(0:4, function(k) {
    formula <- reformulate(c("level", head(paste0("lag", 1:4), k)),
                           response = "change")
    BIC(lm(formula, data = regression_data))
  })
  k <- which.min(bic) - 1
  adf <- ur.df(y, type = "drift", lags = k, selectlags = "Fixed")
  kpss <- ur.kpss(y, type = "mu", lags = "short")
  data.frame(ADF_lags = k, ADF = adf@teststat[1, "tau2"], KPSS = kpss@teststat)
}
tests <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(series), function(j) {
  y <- initial[[series[j]]]
  rbind(cbind(Series = series_names[j], Form = "Level", test_series(y)),
        cbind(Series = series_names[j], Form = "First difference", test_series(diff(y))))
}))
knitr::kable(tests, digits = 3, booktabs = TRUE,
  col.names = c("Series", "Form", "ADF lags", "ADF", "KPSS"),
  caption = "ADF and KPSS tests, 1960Q1-1999Q4.")
```

## Residual diagnostics for the leading Stage 2 one-step model {.unnumbered}

<!-- OWNER: Dawson. Ported from Stage 2, Step 5. -->

Among the estimated models (AR($p$), direct AR, gap AR, Phillips curve), the
gap AR has the lowest one-step RMSE. We refit it on all data through 2019Q4.

```{r}
#| label: step5-refit
h1_rmse <- results |>
  filter(h == 1 & model %in% c("AR(p)", "Direct AR", "Gap AR", "Phillips curve")) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarize(rmse = sqrt(mean(error^2))) |>
  arrange(rmse)
best_model <- h1_rmse |> slice(1) |> pull(model)
stopifnot(best_model == "Gap AR")

train_2019 <- q |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(qtr <= yearquarter("2019 Q4")) |>
  select(qtr, infl, unrate, tbill)
gap_fit <- fit_gap_ar(train_2019)
resid_ts <- gap_fit$resid |> as_tsibble(index = qtr)
lb <- resid_ts |> features(resid, ljung_box, lag = 8, dof = gap_fit$p)
```

BIC selects `r gap_fit$p` gap lags, with coefficients summing to
`r sprintf("%.2f", sum(coef(gap_fit$fit)[-1]))`. The residual standard error is
`r sprintf("%.2f", sigma(gap_fit$fit))` percentage points. The Ljung-Box
statistic is `r sprintf("%.2f", lb$lb_stat)` with `r 8 - gap_fit$p` degrees of
freedom ($p$ = `r sprintf("%.3f", lb$lb_pvalue)`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-step5-resid
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-cap: "Gap AR residuals, refit through 2019Q4 (percentage points)."
resid_ts |>
  autoplot(resid) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual (pp)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-step5-acf
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-cap: "Gap AR residual ACF through 20 quarters. Dashed lines are approximate 95% bounds."
resid_ts |>
  ACF(resid, lag_max = 20) |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(x = "Lag (quarters)", y = "ACF")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-step5-sd
sd_by_period <- resid_ts |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(period = case_when(
    qtr <= yearquarter("1972 Q4") ~ "1960-1972",
    qtr <= yearquarter("1986 Q4") ~ "1973-1986",
    qtr <= yearquarter("2004 Q4") ~ "1987-2004",
    TRUE ~ "2005-2019")) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarize(quarters = n(), sd = sd(resid), max_abs = max(abs(resid)))
knitr::kable(sd_by_period, digits = 2, booktabs = TRUE,
  col.names = c("Period", "Quarters", "Residual SD", "Largest |residual|"),
  caption = "Gap AR residual variability by period.")
```
